AgentForce · Custom Lightning Types

Building Interactive UI in Agent Conversations

AgentForce talks in text by default. For anything more than a quick question, that's a problem. This guide walks through Custom Lightning Types (CLT) — the pattern that lets an agent swap its plain-text replies for a real, schema-driven Lightning form and a styled result card, using a hands-on lead-creation agent as the running example.

⚙ Stack: Apex · Lightning Web Components · Agent Script
🎯 Example used throughout: Lead creation agent
// the problem

Why not just let the agent chat?

AgentForce is conversational by design — the user types a message, the agent replies in text. That's fine for most questions. It breaks down the moment an agent needs structured data across several fields.

Take an enterprise user creating leads all day. Doing that conversationally means one back-and-forth per field — company, then email, then industry, then phone — each one a separate round trip. It's slow, and it wears the user down long before the lead is actually created.

A Custom Lightning Type replaces that whole exchange with one form: text inputs, a combo box, validation, submit — collected in a single shot. The response comes back the same way, as a styled SLDS card instead of a wall of text.

Conversational onlyMany round trips
What's the company name?
Acme Corporation
Got it. What's their email?
info@acme.com
And which industry?
Technology
With a Custom Lightning TypeOne shot
// the architecture

The three-layer model

Every CLT is built as a small pipeline of three layers, each with exactly one job: what data moves and where, how that data connects to a component, and how it actually looks to the user.

1

Agent Script + Apex

Orchestration

Defines what data is collected and where it gets sent.

  • Action definition
  • Input marked is_user_input
  • Output marked is_displayable
  • References a complex_data_type_name
  • Apex service holds the business logic
2

Lightning Type Bundle

Wiring / glue

Connects the Apex data shape to the right LWC — nothing more.

  • schema.json — Apex class reference
  • editor.json — maps input to the editor LWC
  • renderer.json — maps output to the renderer LWC
3

Lightning Web Components

User interface

Decides how it actually looks and behaves for the user.

  • Editor component renders the form, collects input
  • Renderer component receives data via @api
  • Renderer displays it as a styled card

Layer 1 — Agent Script & Apex

In the agent script, each action names which piece of data is input and which is output. The input needs is_user_input: true; the output needs is_displayable: true. Both point at a complex_data_type_name — a wrapper type defined on the Apex side as an @InvocableVariable.

# agent script — action definition
actions:
  create_lead:
    inputs:
      lead_data: object
        complex_data_type_name: "c__leadInput"
        is_user_input: true
    outputs:
      lead_result: object
        complex_data_type_name: "c__leadResult"
        is_displayable: true

Building the Apex service class

The pattern is the same for every CLT you'll ever build: an Apex class with inner classes for the data shapes, plus wrapper classes that carry those shapes across the boundary to the agent script action. LeadCreationService.cls is one Apex class with four inner classes inside it.

Input shape

LeadInput

  • firstName required
  • lastName required
  • company required
  • email
  • phone
  • leadSource
Output shape

LeadResult

  • leadId
  • name, company
  • email, phone
  • status, leadSource
  • createdDate
Request wrapper

CreateLeadRequest

  • lead_data: LeadInput
  • → agent script input param
Response wrapper

CreateLeadResponse

  • lead_result: LeadResult
  • lead_id: String
  • lead_name: String
  • → agent script output params
⚠️

The rule that will burn you

Wrapper field names must be an exact match for the agent script's parameter names. CreateLeadRequest.lead_data only carries data because the action input is also named lead_data — same for lead_result, lead_id and lead_name on the way out. Get a name wrong and nothing throws an error: the field just comes back null, or the agent silently falls back to the plain-text UI.

Building it, step by step

  1. 01
    Create the class
    New Apex class, LeadCreationService.
  2. 02
    Define LeadInput
    One @InvocableVariable per form field. Add required=true on any field that should be mandatory on the UI.
  3. 03
    Define LeadResult
    Plain fields for whatever the confirmation card needs to show — no annotation required, this one only flows outward.
  4. 04
    Define CreateLeadRequest
    One field, lead_data, typed as LeadInput — the name must match the agent script's input parameter.
  5. 05
    Define CreateLeadResponse
    lead_result, lead_id, lead_name — each name must match an agent script output parameter.
  6. 06
    Write createLead() and deploy
    The @InvocableMethod that inserts the Lead, re-queries it for system fields, builds the response, and returns it to the agent.
public with sharing class LeadCreationService {

    // ── CLT INPUT DATA SHAPE ──
    public class LeadInput {
        @InvocableVariable(required=true)
        public String firstName;
        @InvocableVariable(required=true)
        public String lastName;
        @InvocableVariable(required=true)
        public String company;
        @InvocableVariable
        public String email;
        @InvocableVariable
        public String phone;
        @InvocableVariable
        public String leadSource;
    }

    // ── CLT OUTPUT DATA SHAPE ──
    public class LeadResult {
        public Id leadId;
        public String name;
        public String company;
        public String email;
        public String phone;
        public String status;
        public String leadSource;
        public Datetime createdDate;
    }

    // ── REQUEST WRAPPER — field name must match the agent script's input param ──
    public class CreateLeadRequest {
        @InvocableVariable(required=true)
        public LeadInput lead_data;
    }

    // ── RESPONSE WRAPPER — field names must match the agent script's output params ──
    public class CreateLeadResponse {
        public LeadResult lead_result;
        public String lead_id;
        public String lead_name;
    }

    @InvocableMethod(label='Create Lead' description='Creates a new Lead record')
    public static List<CreateLeadResponse> createLead(List<CreateLeadRequest> requests) {
        List<CreateLeadResponse> responses = new List<CreateLeadResponse>();

        for (CreateLeadRequest req : requests) {
            LeadInput input = req.lead_data;

            Lead newLead = new Lead(
                FirstName  = input.firstName,
                LastName   = input.lastName,
                Company    = input.company,
                Email      = input.email,
                Phone      = input.phone,
                LeadSource = input.leadSource
            );
            insert newLead;

            // re-query for system fields (Status, generated Name, CreatedDate)
            Lead created = [
                SELECT Id, Name, Company, Email, Phone, Status, LeadSource, CreatedDate
                FROM Lead
                WHERE Id = :newLead.Id
                LIMIT 1
            ];

            LeadResult result   = new LeadResult();
            result.leadId       = created.Id;
            result.name         = created.Name;
            result.company      = created.Company;
            result.email        = created.Email;
            result.phone        = created.Phone;
            result.status       = created.Status;
            result.leadSource   = created.LeadSource;
            result.createdDate  = created.CreatedDate;

            CreateLeadResponse resp = new CreateLeadResponse();
            resp.lead_result = result;
            resp.lead_id     = created.Id;
            resp.lead_name   = created.Name;

            responses.add(resp);
        }
        return responses;
    }
}

Deploy the class before moving on. Two of these inner classes — LeadInput and LeadResult — are what Layer 2 points at next: when you create a Lightning Type in Setup, its schema is just a reference to one of these classes, addressed as Outer$Inner.

Layer 2 — Lightning Type Bundle

This is the glue between the agent script's data shape and the LWCs that render it. One bundle per direction: an input bundle whose editor.json points at the form component, and an output bundle whose renderer.json points at the display component. Salesforce now lets you assemble these directly from Setup rather than hand-building the bundle.

lightningTypes/ leadInput/ schema.json — Apex class reference editor.json — which LWC renders the form leadResult/ schema.json renderer.json — which LWC renders the card

Layer 3 — Lightning Web Components

The part the user actually sees. The editor component renders the input form and dispatches a valuechange event as the user fills it in. The renderer component receives the finished data through an @api property and displays it as a styled card.

The editor contract

An editor component only works with Agentforce if it honors four rules exactly. Miss one and the platform doesn't error loudly — it just quietly stops passing data.

01 · Meta XML

target = lightning__AgentforceInput

  • targetConfig's property name (not source) set to targetType
02 · Accept

@api value

  • Platform may pass pre-populated or previously entered data when the user navigates back
03 · Accept

@api readOnly

  • Platform sets this true after submission — use it to lock the form
04 · Dispatch

'valuechange' — every field, every time

  • Send the complete object on every change, not just the field that changed
✕ Wrong — dispatch only one field
this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('valuechange', { detail: { lastName: 'Smith' } }));
Result: the platform loses every other field.
firstName lastName company email phone leadSource
✓ Right — dispatch ALL fields every time
this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('valuechange', { detail: this.value // every field }));
Result: the platform keeps the complete, in-sync state.
firstName lastName company email phone leadSource

Building leadInputEditor, step by step

  1. 01
    Scaffold the component
    SFDX: Create Lightning Web Component → leadInputEditor.
  2. 02
    Expose readOnly and value
    @api readOnly = false, plus a getter/setter pair for @api value backed by a private _value.
  3. 03
    Handle every field change
    One handler merges the changed field into _value and dispatches valuechange with the entire object.
  4. 04
    Build the form markup
    A lightning-card, an slds-grid of inputs, one combobox for lead source — every input wired to the same change handler.
  5. 05
    Set the target type in the meta XML
    lightning__AgentforceInput as the target, c__LeadInput as the targetType.
  6. 06
    Deploy, then override the editor in Setup
    Lightning Types → LeadInput → UI Configuration → Editor tab → point it at leadInputEditor instead of the standard component.
leadInputEditor.js
import { LightningElement, api } from 'lwc';

const LEAD_SOURCE_OPTIONS = [
    { label: 'Web', value: 'Web' },
    { label: 'Phone Inquiry', value: 'Phone Inquiry' },
    { label: 'Partner Referral', value: 'Partner Referral' },
    { label: 'Advertisement', value: 'Advertisement' }
];

export default class LeadInputEditor extends LightningElement {
    @api readOnly = false;

    _value = {};

    @api
    get value() {
        return this._value;
    }
    set value(val) {
        this._value = val || {};
    }

    get leadSourceOptions() {
        return LEAD_SOURCE_OPTIONS;
    }

    // fires on every input — always merges into, and sends, the FULL object
    handleChange(event) {
        event.stopPropagation();

        const { name, value } = event.target;
        this._value = { ...this._value, [name]: value };

        this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('valuechange', {
            detail: this._value
        }));
    }
}
leadInputEditor.html
<template>
    <lightning-card title="Create New Lead" icon-name="standard:lead">
        <div class="slds-grid slds-wrap slds-p-around_medium slds-gutters">
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-input label="First Name" name="firstName"
                    value={value.firstName} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-input>
            </div>
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-input label="Last Name" name="lastName" required
                    value={value.lastName} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-input>
            </div>
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-input label="Company" name="company" required
                    value={value.company} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-input>
            </div>
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-input label="Email" name="email" type="email"
                    value={value.email} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-input>
            </div>
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-input label="Phone" name="phone" type="tel"
                    value={value.phone} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-input>
            </div>
            <div class="slds-col slds-size_1-of-2">
                <lightning-combobox label="Lead Source" name="leadSource"
                    placeholder="Select lead source" value={value.leadSource}
                    options={leadSourceOptions} onchange={handleChange} disabled={readOnly}></lightning-combobox>
            </div>
        </div>
    </lightning-card>
</template>
leadInputEditor.js-meta.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<LightningComponentBundle xmlns="http://soap.sforce.com/2006/04/metadata">
    <apiVersion>66.0</apiVersion>
    <isExposed>true</isExposed>
    <masterLabel>Lead Input Editor</masterLabel>
    <targets>
        <target>lightning__AgentforceInput</target>
    </targets>
    <targetConfigs>
        <targetConfig targets="lightning__AgentforceInput">
            <targetType name="c__LeadInput" />
        </targetConfig>
    </targetConfigs>
</LightningComponentBundle>

Deploy, then go back to Setup → Lightning Types → LeadInput → UI Configuration → Editor and override the standard component with c/leadInputEditor. The live preview updates immediately — this is what the platform will actually render.

The renderer contract

The renderer is the easy half. It only ever displays data the platform hands it — no user input, no events, nothing to keep in sync. One rule matters more than the rest: the meta XML uses sourceType, not targetType.

Target

lightning__AgentforceOutput

  • The output counterpart to the editor's ...Input target
Meta config

<sourceType name="..."/>

  • Not targetType — that's the editor's keyword, this is the renderer's
API property

@api value — that's it

  • No readOnly, no getter/setter pair, just one property
Events

None needed

  • The renderer is read-only — nothing to dispatch back

Building leadResultRenderer, step by step

  1. 01
    Scaffold the component
    SFDX: Create Lightning Web Component → leadResultRenderer.
  2. 02
    Expose @api value
    One property — the platform populates it with the LeadResult the Apex service returned.
  3. 03
    Add a getter per field
    Each getter reads off value with a null-safe fallback to '' so the card never shows "undefined".
  4. 04
    Build the confirmation card
    SLDS card + success banner + a details grid — every field bound straight to its getter, nothing interactive.
  5. 05
    Set the source type in the meta XML
    lightning__AgentforceOutput as the target, c__LeadOutput as the sourceType.
  6. 06
    Deploy, then override the renderer in Setup
    Lightning Types → LeadOutput → UI Configuration → Renderer tab → point it at leadResultRenderer.
leadResultRenderer.js
import { LightningElement, api } from 'lwc';

export default class LeadResultRenderer extends LightningElement {
    @api value;

    // null-safe getters — the card renders blank fields instead of "undefined"
    get name()        { return this.value?.name || ''; }
    get company()      { return this.value?.company || ''; }
    get email()        { return this.value?.email || ''; }
    get phone()        { return this.value?.phone || ''; }
    get status()       { return this.value?.status || ''; }
    get leadSource()   { return this.value?.leadSource || ''; }
    get createdDate()  { return this.value?.createdDate || ''; }
}

Layer 3 is complete. The Apex service, both lightning type bundles, and both LWCs are deployed and linked — a user filling out leadInputEditor now flows straight through to a styled card rendered by leadResultRenderer. The only piece left is the agent script that ties the whole pipeline together.

// vocabulary

Key terms

Worth knowing cold before the build — these names show up in the agent script, the bundle, and the Apex class alike.

CLTCustom Lightning Type — the mechanism that swaps an agent's text reply for a real LWC.
complex_data_type_nameThe wrapper type name an action's input or output points at, defined via an Apex @InvocableVariable.
is_user_inputFlag on an action input marking it as data the CLT editor should collect from the user.
is_displayableFlag on an action output marking it as data the CLT renderer should display.
editor.jsonBundle file that maps an input data shape to the LWC responsible for collecting it.
renderer.jsonBundle file that maps an output data shape to the LWC responsible for displaying it.
// worked example

The demo we'll build: lead creation with CLT

Everything in this guide gets applied to one running example — an agent that creates a Salesforce Lead through a real form instead of a chat exchange.

01 · User

Says "create a lead."

02 · Agent

Shows the CLT editor form.

03 · User

Fills all six fields, clicks submit.

04 · Apex

Creates the Lead record.

05 · Agent

Renders a styled confirmation card with the new Lead ID and details.

Components we'll build

  2. 02

// wiring it to agentforce

Creating the agent action asset

Even though the CLT experience gets defined through an agent script, Agentforce still needs a first-class Agent Action asset — the GenAiFunction — that references the Apex invocable method. This is the thing the agent script will actually point at, and it's where the lightning types get attached to the action's inputs and outputs for the first time.

🔗

This is the missing link

The Input Rendering and Output Rendering dropdowns on this asset are where LeadInput and LeadOutput — the lightning types built two sections back — get attached to Create_Lead's parameters. Skip this step and the action still works, but it falls back to the plain-text conversational UI this whole guide exists to avoid.

Building it, step by step

  1. 01
    Open Agentforce Assets
    Setup → quick find asset → Agentforce Studio → Agentforce Assets → Actions → New Agent Action.
  2. 02
    Reference Action Type: Apex
    This action wraps existing functionality rather than defining new logic, so it references what's already deployed.
  3. 03
    Reference Action Category: Invocable Method
    Then pick Create Lead as the Reference Action — the exact @InvocableMethod from LeadCreationService.cls. Label and API name (Create_Lead) autofill.
  4. 04
    Map the input
    lead_data → Data Type @apexClassType/c__LeadCreationService$LeadInput. Check Require input and Collect data from user, then set Input Rendering to LeadInput — that's the lightning type doing the work.
  5. 05
    Map the outputs
    lead_id stays plain text and hidden from the conversation. lead_result gets Data Type c__LeadOutput, Show in conversation checked, and Output Rendering set to LeadOutput.
  6. 06
    Finish
    The asset is saved and ready — this is what the agent script references next.

With Create_Lead saved, every piece is in place: the Apex service, both lightning type bundles, both LWCs, and now the action asset that ties them to a named, invocable action. All that's left is the agent script that calls it.

// the final piece

Writing the agent script

This is where everything gets called. The script welcomes the user, routes to a lead-creation subagent, and — one line matters more than the rest of the file combined — tells Agentforce to render the action as a form instead of asking for each field in plain text.

🔑

The keyword that switches CLT on

Write {!@actions.create_lead} action's user_input tool — not "collect the lead details" or "ask the user for the fields." The platform parses the instruction text for the literal phrase user_input tool; that phrase is the signal that activates the CLT lookup pipeline and finds editor.json. Paraphrase it, and the action still runs — it just falls back to plain-text conversation, with everything else perfectly wired and silently unused.

How the script is organized

Five blocks, top to bottom: system (persona and messages), config (agent identity), variables (session state), a start_agent router, and a subagent that does the actual lead-creation work.

  1. 01
    system + config
    Persona instructions, welcome/error messages, and the agent's label, template, and type.
  2. 02
    variables
    Four mutable variables track session state: lead_created, lead_id, lead_name, create_another.
  3. 03
    start_agent agent_router
    One job: read the message, transition to the lead_creation subagent.
  4. 04
    subagent lead_creation → before_reasoning
    If create_another is true, reset all four variables before reasoning runs again — this is what makes "create another lead" loop cleanly.
  5. 05
    subagent lead_creation → reasoning
    An if/else on lead_created: not yet → call create_lead's user_input tool; already created → report the name and ID, offer to create another.
  6. 06
    subagent lead_creation → actions
    Pulled in from the Create_Lead asset via the + button in the action picker — inputs, outputs, and CLT metadata all come along with it.
⭐

Two habits worth stealing

Keep every identifier in the script lowercase — actions, variables, labels — it's the convention the tooling expects and mismatches are a common source of silent failures. And when an action is referenced inside reasoning (as {!@actions.create_lead}), that name must exactly match the action's own definition below it — same rule as the wrapper-field-name gotcha back in the Apex service.

Pulling the action in from the asset library (rather than hand-typing its metadata) means the inputs and outputs blocks below — is_user_input, complex_data_type_name: "c__LeadInput", is_displayable, complex_data_type_name: "c__LeadOutput" — are copied straight from what was configured two sections ago. Nothing here is retyped by hand.

LeadCreationCLT.agent
system:
    instructions: "You are a sales assistant that helps users create new leads. You use a structured form to collect lead details efficiently. Always be professional and confirm successful creation."
    messages:
        welcome: "Hi! I can help you create a new lead. Just let me know when you are ready.\""
        error: "Something went wrong while creating the lead. Please try again or let me know if you need help with something else."

config:
    agent_label: "LeadCreationCLT"
    agent_template: "EmployeeCopilot__AgentforceEmployeeAgent"
    developer_name: "LeadCreationCLT"
    agent_type: "AgentforceEmployeeAgent"
    description: "Creates leads using Custom Lightning Types for rich form input and styled output display"

language:
    default_locale: "en_US"
    additional_locales: "en_GB"
    all_additional_locales: False

variables:
   lead_created: mutable boolean = False
      description: "Whether a lead has been successfully created this session"
   lead_id: mutable string = ""
      description: "The Salesforce ID of the most recently created lead"
   lead_name: mutable string = ""
      description: "The full name of the most recently created lead"
   create_another: mutable boolean = False
      description: "Whether the user wants to create another lead"

start_agent agent_router:
    description: "Welcome users and route to lead creation workflow"
    reasoning:
        instructions:|
            Select the tool that best matches the user's message and conversation history. If it's unclear, make your best guess.
        actions:
             begin_lead_creation: @utils.transition to @subagent.lead_creation
                description: "Route to lead creation. Call for any lead-related requests including creating, adding, or submitting a new lead."


subagent lead_creation:
    label: "lead_creation"
    description: |

        Collects lead details via a CLT editor form and displays the created lead via a CLT renderer card
    before_reasoning:
        if @variables.create_another:
            set @variables.lead_created = False
            set @variables.lead_id = ""
            set @variables.lead_name = ""
            set @variables.create_another = False
    reasoning:
        instructions: ->
            if not @variables.lead_created:
                | The user wants to create a new lead.
                |  Call {!@actions.create_lead} action's user_input tool to collect the lead details from the user.
                |  Do NOT ask for individual fields via text. Do NOT output any text before showing the form.
                |  If ACTION_CONFIRM, call {!@actions.create_lead} with the form data. Do NOT ask for confirmation or output any text.
            else:
                |   Lead "{!@variables.lead_name}" (ID: {!@variables.lead_id}) was created successfully.
                |   Ask the user if they would like to create another lead or if there is anything else you can help with.
                |   If the user wants to create another lead, call {!@actions.reset_for_new_lead}.
        actions:
            create_lead: @actions.create_lead
                with lead_data = ...
                set @variables.lead_created = True
                set @variables.lead_id = @outputs.lead_id
                set @variables.lead_name = @outputs.lead_result.name
            reset_for_new_lead : @utils.setVariables
                with create_another = true

    actions:
        create_lead:
            description: |
                Creates a new Lead record in Salesforce with the provided details
            label: "Create Lead"
            require_user_confirmation: False
            include_in_progress_indicator: True
            progress_indicator_message: "Creating lead record..."
            source: "Create_Lead"
            target: "apex://LeadCreationService"
                
            inputs:
                "lead_data": object
                    description: |
                      Lead details collected from the form
                              
                    label: "lead_data"
                    is_required: True
                    is_user_input: True
                    complex_data_type_name: "c__LeadInput"
                
            outputs:
                "lead_id": string
                    description: |
                      The ID of the created Lead
                              
                    label: "lead_id"
                    is_displayable: False
                    filter_from_agent: False
                "lead_result": object
                    description: |
                      Created lead details for display
                              
                    label: "lead_result"
                    is_displayable: True
                    filter_from_agent: False
                    complex_data_type_name: "c__LeadOutput"

Save, then hit Preview and say something like "help me create a lead." The structured form appears immediately — no back-and-forth, no field-by-field prompting — and submitting it returns the styled confirmation card straight from leadResultRenderer, exactly like the flow sketched all the way back at the top of this guide.

⚡

The pipeline, end to end

All seven pieces are built and wired: LeadCreationService.cls defines the shapes and the business logic, LeadInput/LeadOutput bind those shapes to components, leadInputEditor and leadResultRenderer render them, Create_Lead exposes it as an action, and LeadCreationCLT.agent calls that action with the one phrase — user_input tool — that switches the whole thing on. A user says "create a lead," fills one form, and gets one styled card back. That's the CLT pattern, in full.
